cells.tense: Care is moving through your hands right now, and the timing is holding.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you look after — plant, person, project — and leave it alone for a day this week. See what carries itself.
cells.core:
You're looking after something real, and you're learning from it as you go. Not reading about it — noticing what it does when you pay attention, adjusting, letting it teach you its own pace. That's the whole method, and it's working. What makes it hold is that you're not gripping. You put the work in, you let the thing answer on its own schedule, and you're steady about the gap between them. Care that doesn't exhaust. Space held without clutching.

What's arriving now is more of this, and the way through is to keep one hand off it. Let something finish without you on top of it. You'll know it when what you've been tending lets go on its own, not when you decide it's done.
cells.sheetLine: You look after it, it answers, and you don't grip.
cells.verb: tending something slowly enough to learn how it actually grows

cells.tense: You're already bracing for a harvest that isn't due yet.
cells.ask: Name the outcome you're pushing toward, then leave it alone today. Do only what today's version of the task needs.
cells.core:
You're running ahead of what you're growing. Checking it too often, adjusting too fast, holding a shape it hasn't reached yet — and care has turned into management. Somewhere ahead is the version where it's finished and flourishing, and you're living there instead of here. That's the cost: the pushing is what's stalling the growth.

What's arriving now doesn't need you to force it. It needs you to let it arrive. Back off long enough that the thing can do what it does without your hand on it every hour. That's not neglect — it's the trust the whole thing runs on. When you can dream about where it's going without needing to drag it there, you'll know the grip has loosened.

cells.tense: You stopped tending it a while back, and you've been standing at a closed door since.
cells.ask: Pick one small living thing and give it ten minutes of plain attention today. Put your hands on it. Say its name.
cells.core:
You knew how to grow things once, and at some point it stopped paying off, so you stepped away. Now what's arriving comes and you watch it from a distance. The hands know what to do; they just don't reach anymore. It isn't a matter of having forgotten how. It's that you stopped showing up to something that answers back.

The way out isn't to feel your way back in — it's to do one small piece of the work first and let the rest catch up. Ten minutes on something alive. Attending to it badly is fine. Development does the rest: the shine comes after you've cultivated something, not before. Small, real, today — that's the whole instruction.

cells.tense: You're already growing something, and you talk about it like weather that happened to you.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that you're the one who grew it — the part that was yours, not the luck.
cells.core:
You are looking after something — steadily, daily, in ways you'd wave off if asked. It's growing because of attention you're giving it. But you describe it as just how things went, or the thing doing it on its own, or nothing worth mentioning. That part is real and running; you just aren't saying so.

That matters here, because what's entering comes through the hands you won't put your name on. Settle one piece of it: that this grew because you showed up for it. Not the whole harvest — the part that was yours. Once you own what you did, the thing can finish, and you can let it finish without needing to pretend you weren't there.

The reader could rightly say 'nothing is arriving,' and the asks survive that because they act on how the person meets what's already in front of them rather than promising an arrival. The sentence that serves the writer is any line that leans on the draw's poetry ('the Apprentice,' 'the material world') — kept out of all four cells.
